title: Thematic review series: brain Lipids. Cholesterol metabolism in the central nervous system during early development and in the mature animal
funder: The original research from this laboratory reviewed in the paper was supported by Grants R37 HL-09610 and T32 DK-07745 from the National Institutes of Health and by a grant from the Moss Heart Fund.
result: Review. In humans the mean concentration of unesterified cholesterol in the central nervous system (about 23 mg/g) is higher than in any other tissue, mostly in compact myelin; the CNS is 2.1% of body weight but contains 23% of the whole-body sterol pool. The cholesterol for CNS growth apparently comes exclusively from synthesis within it, and there is no evidence of net transfer of sterol from blood into brain or spinal cord; in adults synthesis exceeds need and cholesterol leaves the CNS, partly as 24(S)-hydroxycholesterol. Turnover of the CNS sterol pool is about 0.03% a day in the human brain against 0.7% a day for the whole body. The authors state that there is no evidence that plasma cholesterol directly influences CNS cholesterol metabolism, that all orally given statins partially inhibit cholesterol synthesis in the CNS, and that small changes in plasma 24(S)-hydroxycholesterol after statins cannot be proven to reflect changes in its CNS production; whether plasma cholesterol changes affect cognition or dementia remained uncertain.
